art.text: The Anubanini rock relief, carved by the mountain kingdom of Lullubi around 2300 BC, is one of the earliest rock reliefs of Iran. It stands in Kermanshah province. Carved into the rock, it started a sculptural tradition that lasted for many centuries.

In Persian art, large carved rock reliefs were typically placed high beside a road, near a source of water. They were mostly used to glorify the king and proclaim control over territory. The tradition begins with Lullubi and Elamite rock reliefs.

At Tureng Tepe in northeastern Iran, an enormous high terrace of mud bricks was built in the center of the settlement around 2600 to 2100 BC. It may be the earliest example of monumental architecture in its region. Radiocarbon dating placed it between 2550 BC and 2185 BC.

Far to the southeast near Jiroft, archaeologists uncovered a windowed, two-story citadel at Konar Sandal B covering nearly 13.5 hectares. It was part of a city that flourished between 2500 and 2200 BCE.

The Anubanini rock relief is thought to have influenced the later Achaemenid Behistun reliefs, made about a millennium and a half afterwards. The Behistun relief and inscription, created around 500 BC for Darius the Great, is on a far grander scale, proclaiming the power of the Achaemenid Empire.

The Bronze Age settlement at Tureng Tepe, whose name means 'Hill of the Pheasants', dates from about 3100 to 2900 BC through 1900 BC. When Frederick Wulsin excavated in 1931, the surface of Mound C held 75 Bronze Age graves associated with architectural remains.

Bronze objects from Lorestān dating between the fourth millennium BC and the Iranian Bronze Age (c. 2900 to 1250 BC) were broadly similar to those from Mesopotamia and the Iranian Plateau. This included pieces from the Elamite Empire, which covered Lorestān. As in later pieces, animals were a very common subject in small bronzes.

Elamite rock reliefs at Sarpol-e Zahab in Iranian Kurdistan date to circa 2000 BC. Others at Kul-e Farah and Eshkaft-e Salman in southwest Iran belong to the same tradition, which later continued under the Assyrians.

Frederick Wulsin dug a 17 meter deep pit at the top of Mound A at Tureng Tepe to explore a large brick structure eroding out of the mound. The building had two settlement layers and sat on an extensive mudbrick platform.

Frederick Wulsin's 1931 excavations at Tureng Tepe turned up grey burnished ware, red ware, and red ware with black painted decoration. One example of cream colored ware with black painted decoration was also found. A number of the finds ended up at the Penn Museum.

war.text: One of the earliest wars recorded in this region took place in 2700 BCE. King En-me-barage-si of Kish fought Susa and, according to ancient records, made the land of Elam submit.
Around 1320 BCE, the Kassite king of Babylon, Kurigalzu II, temporarily occupied Elam. He had earlier been installed on the throne by Ashur-uballit I of the Middle Assyrian Empire.
Elam did not always have the upper hand over Mesopotamia. Sumerian rulers Eannatum of Lagash and Lugal-anne-mundu of Adab are both recorded as having temporarily dominated Elam.

Even earlier, the Akkadian king Manishtushu claimed to have subjugated Anshan. As Akkad weakened, Kutik-Inshushinak, the governor of Susa and a scion of the Awan dynasty, broke free and captured Anshan for himself.
The rivalry continued: around 1230 BCE, Kassite king Kashtiliash IV attacked Elam but failed to defeat it. Kassite-Babylonian power over the region was already beginning to wane.
In 2200 BCE, Gudea of Lagash claimed to have subjugated Anshan. Later, the Neo-Sumerian kings Shulgi and Shu-Sin of Ur maintained their own governors there.
Elam struck back under King Kiddin-Khutran, who defeated the Kassite king Enlil-nadin-shumi in 1224 BCE. He then defeated another Kassite king, Adad-shuma-iddina, around 1222 to 1217 BCE.

In 2004 BCE, Elam sacked the great Mesopotamian city of Ur, the end of King Ibbi-Sin's long and losing struggle to keep control of Anshan. The Elamites captured Ibbi-Sin himself and took him, along with the statue of Nanna, away to Anshan.

literature.text: The oldest known writing system from ancient Iran, the Proto-Elamite script, was used only briefly, around 3100 to 2900 BC, on clay tablets found across the region. It had more than 1,000 signs, was mostly logographic, and remains undeciphered to this day.
In Elam, in what is now western Iran, written records first appear around 3000 BC. This closely parallels the history of nearby Sumer, where slightly earlier records survive.

Linear Elamite was a writing system used in Elam roughly between 2300 and 1850 BCE, known mainly from a handful of monumental inscriptions. Some scholars argue it is the oldest known purely phonographic, or sound-based, writing system in the world.

At Tepe Yahya, archaeologists found the oldest recovered clay tablets written in Proto-Elamite script. Three tablets from the IVC strata were radiocarbon dated, giving dates of 2955 BC, 2790 BC, and 3490 BC.

Around 2100 BC, Susa's governor Kutik-Inshushinak rebelled against Akkadian rule, turning the city into an independent state and a literary center. He also encouraged the use of the Linear Elamite script, which remains undeciphered.
From about 2500 BC, Elam adopted Elamite cuneiform, a script adapted from Akkadian cuneiform. It functioned as a syllabary of roughly 130 signs and kept only a few logograms borrowed from Akkadian.

Before Elamite language use grew dominant, most written documents from Susa were in Akkadian. The surrounding region of Susiana had been incorporated into Sargon the Great's Akkadian Empire around 2330 BC.

The earliest known Elamite cuneiform text is a treaty dating to around 2200 BC between the Akkadian king Nāramsîn and the Elamite ruler Hita. Its surviving lines read like a mutual pledge: 'Nāramsîn's friend is my friend, Nāramsîn's enemy is my enemy.'

After King Puzur-Shushinak, the last ruler of the Awan Dynasty, died around 2100 BCE, Susa was overrun by the Third Dynasty of Ur while the rest of Elam came under the Shimashki dynasty. Despite this upheaval, the Linear Elamite script continued to be used.

Beyond Susa, texts in the undeciphered Proto-Elamite script have also turned up at Tepe Sofalin and Tepe Yahya. Another key site, Tepe Sialk, holds the only Proto-Elamite ziggurat still standing today.

Around 2100 BC, Susa's governor Kutik-Inshushinak rebelled against Akkadian rule and made the city an independent state. He also encouraged the use of the Linear Elamite script, a writing system that remains undeciphered today.

The earliest known text in Elamite cuneiform, adapted from Akkadian cuneiform, is a treaty between the Akkadian king Naram-Sin and the Elamite ruler Khita, dating to around 2250 BC. Elamite cuneiform eventually became a syllabary of about 130 signs.

Under the Igehalkid dynasty, which ruled Elam from about 1400 to 1210 BC, Akkadian-language inscriptions became rare at Susa. In their place, Elamite highland gods and, with them, the Elamite language became firmly established.

The undeciphered Proto-Elamite script survives on tablets from only five known sites. Unusually, alongside the standard sexagesimal, or base-60, counting system, its scribes also used a base-120 system and a decimal system.

science.text: Iran's oldest known writing system, Proto-Elamite script, was used from about 3100 to 2900 BC on clay tablets found across ancient Iran. It had more than 1,000 signs, was mostly logographic, and has never been deciphered.

The Proto-Elamite script, used in the early Bronze Age before Elamite cuneiform, remains largely undeciphered except for its numbers. Unusually, it combined the usual sexagesimal and base-120 numbering systems with an additional decimal system, all within the same set of records.

Tepe Yahya, a Bronze Age site in southeastern Iran, was a center of early metallurgy. Archaeologists found several metal artifacts there, including a copper shaft-hole axe, a copper spearhead, and a copper and lead figurine shaped like an animal.

In the middle of the 2nd millennium BC, Tepe Yahya became a production center for carved chlorite stone vessels known as chlorite stoneware. These dark stone vessels were valued widely enough to be found in ancient Mesopotamian temples.
Tepe Yahya yielded some of the oldest known clay tablets written in Proto-Elamite script. Radiocarbon dating of three tablets from the site's IVC layer gave dates of 2955 BC, 2790 BC, and 3490 BC.

At Susa, capital of ancient Elam, copper metallurgy was already practiced in the Susa I period, contemporary with metalworking at other Iranian sites such as Tepe Sialk. Centuries later, in the Susa III or 'Proto-Elamite' period, lasting from about 3100 to 2700 BC, the first Proto-Elamite tablets appear.

More than 1,000 steatite pieces have been found at Tepe Yahya, and archaeologists discovered a steatite mine near the site, showing the vessels were made locally. These carved stone vessels traveled remarkably far, turning up as far away as Mohenjodaro in India.

politics.text: The Awan dynasty was the first known dynasty of Elam, appearing at the dawn of recorded history around 2400 BC. It was later succeeded first by the Shimashki dynasty and then by the Sukkalmah dynasty as rulers of Elam.

Susa served as the capital of Elam, one of the most important cities of the Ancient Near East. The Old Elamite period began around 2700 BC when Elam was conquered by Enmebaragesi, the Sumerian king of Kish.

Around 2240 BC, as the Akkadian empire started to break down, Kutik-Inshushinak, the governor of Susa on behalf of Akkad, liberated Awan and Elam and ascended to the throne. He defeated the rebelling neighbouring towns of Kimash and Hurtum, destroying 70 cities in a day, then defeated all his rivals and took Anshan, the capital. He launched a campaign of devastation throughout northern Sumer, seizing cities such as Eshnunna, and when he finally conquered Akkad he was declared king of the four quarters, owner of the known world.

The Shimashki confederacy of Elam led an alliance against the Ur III Empire and defeated its last ruler, Ibbi-Sin. After this victory they destroyed the kingdom and looted the capital city of Ur. They then ruled through military occupation for the next 21 years.
The Igehalkid dynasty ruled Elam from about 1400 to 1210 BC and had at least ten known rulers. Some of these Igehalkid rulers married Kassite princesses.
The Shimashkian king Kindattu led the army that destroyed the Third Dynasty of Ur in 2004 BC. This was a joint operation with his ally Ishbi-Erra, and together they captured Ibbi-Sin, the king of Ur.

King Ibbi-Sin of Ur spent his reign struggling unsuccessfully to maintain control over Anshan. This ended in the Elamite sack of Ur in 2004 BC, when the statue of the god Nanna, and Ibbi-Sin himself, were captured and taken to Anshan.
Idaddu I, also known as Indattu, called himself king of Shimashki and Elam. He is said to have ascended the throne of Shimashki around 1970 BC, possibly as the son or grandson of Kindattu.

philosophy.text: According to the Oxford Dictionary of Philosophy, the chronology of philosophy as a subject starts with the Indo-Iranians. It dates this event to 1500 BC. Iranian philosophy is traced back to Old Iranian traditions that grew from ancient Indo-Iranian roots.

The teachings of Zarathustra appeared in Persia at some point during the period 1700-1800 BCE. His wisdom became the basis of the religion Zoroastrianism. It also influenced the development of the Iranian branch of Indo-Iranian philosophy.

Before Zoroastrianism, the Iranian peoples had their own set of beliefs and practices, now called ancient Iranian religion. The closest religion to it was the Vedic religion of India. The Iranian peoples emerged as a separate branch of the Indo-Iranians in the 2nd millennium BC.

Zarathustra was the first to treat the problem of evil in philosophical terms. His approach became part of the Iranian branch of Indo-Iranian philosophy. It gave Zoroastrianism a lasting place in the story of philosophy.
Zarathustra espoused an ethical philosophy built on the primacy of good thoughts, good words and good deeds. In Persian these are andiše-e-nik, goftâr-e-nik and kerdâr-e-nik.

During the first half of the 2nd millennium BC, one group of Indo-Europeans migrated south from the Central Asian Steppe into the Iranian plateau and the Indian subcontinent. Scholars call them the Indo-Iranians. They eventually branched into the Indo-Aryan peoples and the Iranian peoples.

The major deities worshipped in ancient Iranian religion were Ahura Mazda and Mithra, though Atar was also worshipped. This is known because names of kings and common people showing devotion to these three exist in most cases.

Because Iranian and Indo-Aryan religion share a common origin, they are substantially similar. Comparing both groups lets scholars reconstruct general features of Iranian religion for which there is no direct documentation.

With the rise of Zoroaster and his new, reformatory religion, Ahura Mazda became the principal deity. The Daevas were relegated to the background. Some earlier sects, the precursors of the Magi, had also worshipped Ahura Mazda.

Many of the attributes and commandments of Varuna, called Fahrana in Median times, were later attributed to Ahura Mazda by Zoroaster. This shows how older Iranian ideas about a divine figure were carried into the new religion.

culture.text: Iran is the place of origin of complex musical instruments, with some dating back to the 3rd millennium BC. Several trumpets made of silver, gold and copper were found in eastern Iran and attributed to the Oxus civilization. They date to between 2200 and 1750 BC.

In the 2nd millennium BC the Iranian peoples emerged as a separate branch of the Indo-Iranians and came to dominate the Eurasian Steppe and the Persian Plateau. They left little written or material evidence of their religion. Scholars reconstruct it from scant Iranian, Babylonian and Greek accounts and from similarities with the Vedic religion.

According to Geoffrey Summers, Kura–Araxes peoples moved into Iran and the Van region quite suddenly, starting shortly before 3000 BC. He suggests the move may have been prompted by the Late Uruk Collapse, which ended the Uruk IV phase around 3100 BC.
Local versions of the Kura–Araxes culture were known by different names. One of them, the Yanik Tepe culture, is named for a site in Iranian Azerbaijan, near Lake Urmia.
The name Kura–Araxes was coined by Boris Kuftin in 1940 and comes from the Kura and Araxes river valleys. Other local variations are sometimes called Shengavitian, Karaz and Pulur cultures.
